title: Minoan Crete
description: From the first farmers at Knossos to the palaces, the eruption of Thera and the mainland Greeks who took Crete over: Europe’s first palace civilisation, and how it was found.
note: Minoan dates come from pottery styles and radiocarbon and are approximate; the date of the Thera eruption is disputed by about a century. The Minoans’ own language is unknown, so native names are the later Greek ones, or Linear B forms where the tablets give them.

steps.title: A mound of farmers
steps.text: Some of the first farmers in the Aegean crossed to Crete by boat, bringing wheat, barley, sheep, goats, pigs and cattle. They settled on a low hill at Knossos about 7000 BCE. For thousands of years their houses of mud brick were rebuilt on the ruins of the last, raising a mound several metres deep beneath the later palace.
steps.today: Today: the Neolithic levels lie under the palace at Knossos, 5 km south of Heraklion, Crete.

steps.title: Gold of the tombs
steps.text: In the Early Bronze Age, villages spread along Crete’s coasts and plains. On Mochlos, then a headland, families buried their dead in stone house-tombs, used over generations. They held gold diadems, flower-shaped hairpins and bands, carved stone vases and seals. The gold and the stones came from overseas, so Cretans were already trading across the Aegean.
steps.today: Today: an islet off Mochlos village, eastern Crete. Rising seas have cut it off from the shore.

steps.title: The first palace
steps.text: About 1900 BCE, buildings arranged around a great paved central court rise at Knossos, and soon after at Phaistos and Malia. Archaeologists call them palaces, though no one knows who ruled from them: a king, a priesthood or a council. Their rows of storerooms held oil, grain and wine, gathered from the land around.
steps.today: Today: the palace at Knossos, Crete’s most visited ancient site. Most of what is seen is the second palace.

steps.title: Pots as thin as eggshell
steps.text: Phaistos, on a ridge above the fertile Mesara plain, had its own palace and potters’ workshops. Kamares ware, named after the cave on Mount Ida where it was first found, was made on the fast wheel with walls as thin as eggshell, painted in white, red and orange spirals on a dark ground. It reached Egypt and the Levant.
steps.today: Today: the palace site at Phaistos, south-central Crete. The finds are in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

steps.title: The bee pendant
steps.text: The palace at Malia stands on the north coast, on a plain between the mountains and the sea. In the nearby burial ground of Chrysolakkos, a gold pendant was found showing two bees, or wasps, holding a drop of honey between them. Its makers used granulation, fusing tiny gold beads onto a surface, a skill learned from the Near East.
steps.today: Today: the palace site near Malia, east of Heraklion. The bee pendant is in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

steps.title: Gods on the mountaintops
steps.text: Minoans worshipped on mountain peaks. On the summit of Juktas, in sight of Knossos, people left clay figures of worshippers, animals and even single limbs, perhaps asking for healing. Who they prayed to is unknown. Much later, Cretans pointed out Juktas as the grave of Zeus, a claim other Greeks mocked as a Cretan lie.
steps.today: Today: Mount Giouchtas, south of Heraklion. A chapel stands on the summit beside the sanctuary’s remains.

steps.title: Signs no one can read
steps.text: Minoan scribes wrote in two scripts, Cretan hieroglyphic and then Linear A, on clay tablets, seals and offerings. Neither has been deciphered, and the language is unknown. At Phaistos, archaeologists found a clay disc stamped with 242 signs in a spiral on both faces, the Phaistos Disc. Its date, meaning and even its purpose are still argued over.
steps.today: Today: the Phaistos Disc is in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum; many Linear A tablets come from Hagia Triada, near Phaistos.

steps.title: Palace of light and colour
steps.text: Earthquakes wrecked the first palaces about 1700 BCE, and greater ones were built on their ruins. Knossos rose several storeys around its court, with grand staircases, light wells, drains and flushing channels. Its walls were painted with processions, lilies, monkeys and youths leaping over bulls. Estimates of the town around it range from about 10,000 people to over 20,000.
steps.today: Today: Knossos, as partly rebuilt in concrete by Arthur Evans in the 1920s; the original frescoes are in Heraklion.

steps.title: A town of workshops
steps.text: Gournia shows how ordinary Minoans lived. Narrow paved lanes climb a low hill past small stone houses, each with storerooms below and living rooms above. Carpenters, potters, weavers and a metalworker left their tools behind. A small palace with a court stands at the top. It was excavated by Harriet Boyd between 1901 and 1904.
steps.today: Today: the site of Gournia, beside the coast road above the Gulf of Mirabello, eastern Crete.

steps.title: The unplundered palace
steps.text: Zakros, on a sheltered bay facing east, was Crete’s door to Cyprus, the Levant and Egypt. When it burned about 1450 BCE, no one came back to dig through the ruins. Nikolaos Platon found it untouched in 1962: stone vases, a rock crystal ritual vessel, copper ingots and elephant tusks from the east, all where they fell.
steps.today: Today: the palace site at Kato Zakros, at the end of a gorge on Crete’s east coast.

steps.title: Men of Keftiu in Egypt
steps.text: Egyptian records name a land of Keftiu, which most scholars identify as Crete. In the Theban tomb of Rekhmire, vizier of Thutmose III, men of Keftiu bring tall vases and metal cups as gifts. Their kilts were later repainted in a mainland Greek style. In the delta at Avaris, Egyptian buildings were painted with Minoan-style bull-leaping scenes.
steps.today: Today: the tomb of Rekhmire at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, on the west bank at Luxor. Kommos is a beach site south of Phaistos.

steps.title: Minoan ways overseas
steps.text: Minoan pottery, Linear A and Cretan ways of building, weaving and worship spread to Kythera, Rhodes, Thera and Miletus on the Anatolian coast. Scholars debate whether these were Cretan colonies or local towns copying Crete. Much later the Athenian historian Thucydides wrote that Minos was the first to rule the sea with a navy, a story he took from tradition.
steps.today: Today: the ruins of Miletus near Balat, western Turkey. The coast has silted up and now lies 8 km away.

steps.title: The painted town of Thera
steps.text: On the island of Thera, Akrotiri was a busy harbour town of two and three storey houses, paved streets and drains, close to Crete in its art and writing. Its walls were painted with swallows among lilies, boys boxing, young women gathering saffron and a fleet sailing between towns. Spyridon Marinatos began uncovering it in 1967.
steps.today: Today: Akrotiri, under a protective roof on the south coast of Santorini, Greece.

steps.title: The eruption
steps.when: about 1600 BCE by radiocarbon, or about 1500 BCE by pottery dating; disputed
steps.text: Earthquakes warned Akrotiri’s people, who left with their valuables; no bodies have been found. Then the volcano erupted, one of the largest of the last 10,000 years, burying the town in ash and leaving the island’s flooded crater. Ash fell on Crete and waves struck its north coast. Yet the Cretan palaces carried on for generations afterwards.
steps.today: Today: the caldera of Santorini, the flooded crater the eruption left. Its date is still argued over by about a century.

steps.title: Mainland lords at Knossos
steps.text: About 1450 BCE, fire destroyed palaces, villas and towns across Crete, Zakros, Malia, Phaistos and Gournia among them. Knossos alone carried on, now under rulers whose records are in Greek and whose warrior graves resemble those of mainland Mycenae. Whether they came as invaders, took power after earthquake or revolt, or were invited in is disputed.
steps.today: Today: Mycenae, in the Argolid, Greece. Warrior graves of this period lie around Knossos.

steps.title: Tablets baked by fire
steps.when: about 1400 to 1350 BCE, or later; disputed
steps.text: When Knossos burned, the fire baked thousands of clay tablets in the Linear B script, adapted from Linear A to write Greek. They count around 100,000 sheep for wool, plus linen, chariots and offerings to the gods, and name places such as Phaistos (pa-i-to). Michael Ventris showed in 1952 that the language was an early Greek.
steps.today: Today: the Knossos tablets are in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. When the archive burned is still argued over.

steps.title: Into the hills
steps.text: Around 1200 BCE, palaces across the eastern Mediterranean fell, and Crete’s people moved up to defensible heights. At Karfi, a windswept peak over 1,100 metres high, a village of about 150 houses kept a shrine with clay goddesses raising their arms. By about 1000 BCE the Bronze Age world of Crete had ended.
steps.today: Today: the peak of Karfi, above Tzermiado on the Lasithi plateau. A rough path leads up to the ruins.

steps.title: Where Zeus was hidden
steps.text: Greek tradition says the god Zeus was born in a Cretan cave and hidden there from his father Kronos, who swallowed his children. Two caves claim him: the Dictaean Cave at Psychro and the Idaean Cave on Mount Ida. Bronze double axes and figures left at Psychro show it was a place of worship in Minoan times.
steps.today: Today: the Psychro cave above the Lasithi plateau, open to visitors, with stalagmites in its lower hall.

steps.title: Minos and the Minotaur
steps.text: In Greek tradition, Minos, son of Zeus, ruled Crete. His wife bore the Minotaur, half bull, kept in a maze (labyrinth) built by Daedalus. Athens sent youths to feed it until Theseus killed it, helped by Ariadne’s thread. A Knossos tablet names a Mistress of the Labyrinth, but whether the palace inspired the myth is not known.
steps.today: Today: the palace at Knossos, whose maze of rooms many visitors take for the labyrinth.

steps.title: Digging up Minos
steps.text: Minos Kalokairinos, a Heraklion merchant, first dug at Knossos in 1878 and found storerooms of giant jars. In 1900, Arthur Evans bought the site and uncovered the palace. He named its people Minoans, after Minos. What they called themselves is unknown. His concrete rebuildings of the 1920s still shape, and still divide, how visitors see Knossos.
steps.today: Today: the Knossos site and the Heraklion Archaeological Museum, which holds most Minoan finds.

facts.Trade: Traded with Crete, which it called Keftiu.

facts.Writing: Linear B, an early form of Greek

rulers.text: Not named; the Linear B title was wanax (“king”)

items.name: Minos
items.role: King of Crete in Greek tradition
items.text: In Greek tradition, Minos was a son of Zeus and Europa who ruled Crete from Knossos and made laws so just that he became a judge of the dead. Thucydides credits him with the first navy. Whether any real king lies behind the name is unknown; it may even have been a title rather than a name.

items.name: Harriet Boyd Hawes
items.text: Harriet Boyd led the excavation of Gournia from 1901 to 1904, among the first women to direct a major dig in the Mediterranean. Her team uncovered a whole Minoan town, and her 1908 report on it set a standard for publishing a site. She also served as a volunteer nurse in several wars.

items.name: Luigi Pernier
items.text: Luigi Pernier worked with Federico Halbherr on the Italian excavations at Phaistos from 1900. On 3 July 1908, digging in a storeroom of the palace, he found the clay disc stamped with signs that has puzzled scholars ever since. He later directed the Italian archaeological school at Athens.

items.name: Minos Kalokairinos
items.text: Minos Kalokairinos, a merchant of Heraklion, dug at Knossos in 1878 and found storerooms lined with great clay jars. The Ottoman authorities stopped the work. In 1898 his house and much of his collection were destroyed by fire during fighting in Heraklion. He is often left out of the story Evans told.

items.name: Arthur Evans
items.text: Arthur Evans, keeper of the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, was drawn to Crete by its sealstones. He dug at Knossos from 1900, named the Minoans and published The Palace of Minos in four volumes from 1921 to 1935. His reconstructions in concrete made the site vivid, but are criticised for guessing too much.

items.name: Spyridon Marinatos
items.text: Spyridon Marinatos argued in 1939 that the eruption of Thera had struck Minoan Crete. From 1967 he excavated Akrotiri, uncovering its houses and wall paintings. Later dating showed the palaces outlived the eruption by generations. He died at the site in 1974 after a fall, and is buried there.

items.name: Michael Ventris
items.text: Michael Ventris, an architect who had been fascinated by Linear B since boyhood, showed in 1952 that it wrote an early form of Greek. With the scholar John Chadwick he published the decipherment in 1953. He died in a road accident in 1956, aged 34. Linear A, the Minoan script, remains unread.
